questions.q: Why does the fast food industry market so heavily to children?
a: They are easy to persuade and can pressure parents into buying
They have their own money and decide what the family eats
They are the only group still eating inside restaurants
They respond better to serious, information-heavy advertising
questions.why: Lesson 1 says children are impressionable and can annoy parents into paying.

questions.q: What tends to happen to a town after a large meatpacking plant moves in?
a: Crime and demand for subsidized medical care rise sharply
Wages rise and long-term residents return to the area
Local farms expand and food prices fall for everyone
Schools and public services improve almost immediately
questions.why: Lesson 2 cites Lexington, Nebraska, where both doubled within a decade.

questions.q: Which health problem does the summary call worse than obesity?
a: Food poisoning from contaminated meat, striking 130,000 people daily
A rise in childhood asthma linked to restaurant fumes
Vitamin deficiencies caused by eating only burgers
Hearing loss from noisy fast food kitchens
questions.why: Lesson 3 says E. coli in mass-produced meat sickens 130,000 Americans a day.

questions.q: How does the meat industry keep its labor costs so low?
a: It hires desperate workers and releases them before benefits begin
It trains skilled workers and pays them by the hour
It relies on robots for nearly every stage of processing
It offers permanent contracts to attract experienced staff
questions.why: Lesson 2 describes firing workers just before six months to avoid insurance.

questions.q: Why can a single contaminated batch of meat reach millions of people?
a: Only four large companies supply most of the country's meat
Meat is shipped abroad before any safety checks occur
Restaurants refuse to buy from local independent farms
Inspectors sample only one burger per state each year
questions.why: Lesson 3 points to the extreme concentration of meat packing in four firms.
